runs.text: A Task per filesystem event: 190 000 suspended tasks, 638 MB, and ten pinned cores

A dev build left open for eleven hours on two repositories held 803 MB and burned 329% CPU with nothing on screen doing anything. The leak was not in the Rust core, which the process spends all its time inside. It was one unstructured
per filesystem event, and the generation counter that looks like it guards against exactly this and does not.

runs.text: About 190 000 suspended tasks, 638 MB of task stacks. That count is the whole diagnosis: it is not one runaway scan, it is eleven hours of arrivals that were never served and never dropped.
Two independent faults that only bite together.
The model queued a task per event and cancelled none.
walk. The generation counter reads like a guard against pile-up. It is not: it discards a stale
, and does nothing about the work producing it. The detached walk runs to completion regardless, and
starts a stash load beside it. Nothing bounds how many are outstanding.
Each walk was an order of magnitude slower than it had to be.

for each entry and skips the hash when it still matches disk. On a 13 185-file checkout that was 1.8–2.8 s per walk against

Put together they cross a threshold. FSEvents coalesces at a 0.5 s latency, so a working tree under churn — a build, a dev server, a watch process — delivers roughly one callback a second. A walk that takes longer than the interval between arrivals is a queue that never drains: the pool runs ten at a time forever and every further request is added to a backlog whose only bound is memory. Halve the arrival rate or halve the service time and the process looks fine for hours; it is the crossing that turns a spike into eleven hours of accumulation.

The Rust side is not the leak. Ten concurrent walks in a standalone harness hold at 52 MB across repeated rounds. The memory is entirely the Swift task backlog, which is why nothing in the core's own budgets or tests caught it.
1. Coalesce in the model; never queue.
One scan in flight plus at most one queued re-run, however many requests arrive:
Both flags are only read and written on the main actor with no suspension between the loop's

check and the assignment that follows it, so a request that arrives during a scan always lands in the flag the scan is about to read. Nothing is lost and nothing stacks. The cost is that returning no longer means "your scan finished" — it means the model has accounted for it. Say so in the doc comment; a caller that assumes otherwise is the next bug.
2. Read the index as a stat cache.

— a cache that answers on partial evidence hides a real edit, which is far worse than a slow scan.
3. Cancel what can be cancelled, and say what cannot.

A generation counter is not backpressure. It decides which result is allowed to land; it says nothing about how much work is running. Any load driven by a watcher needs an explicit in-flight flag as well.

time. A walk twice as fast is worth less than one that cannot be asked for twice at once, and a system where arrivals outpace service degrades without bound rather than gracefully.
